title: YOU HAVE A WIFE—SO WHY ARE YOU STILL COURTING OTHER WOMEN?
paragraphs: YOU HAVE A WIFE—SO WHY ARE YOU STILL COURTING OTHER WOMEN?

You may never have touched her. You may never have kissed her. But if you are deliberately pursuing another woman’s heart while your wife is waiting for yours, Jesus has something painfully serious to say.
There is a kind of betrayal that happens long before two bodies ever meet.
It begins with a message you would rather your wife not see.
A conversation you delete.
A compliment that carries more intention than you want to admit.
A “good morning” message that somehow became daily.
An inside joke your wife knows nothing about.
A woman whose notification makes something inside you come alive.
You tell yourself, “We’re only talking.”
“She’s just a friend.”
“I haven’t slept with anybody.”
“I know my limits.”
But perhaps that is not the most important question.
The question is this:
Why are you trying to awaken in another woman something that belongs inside the covenant you already made with your wife?
That question hurts because sometimes we rename sin before we repent of it.
We call lust “admiration.”
We call flirting “being friendly.”
We call emotional dependency “just talking.”
We call secrecy “privacy.”
We call pursuing another woman “nothing serious.”
And sometimes the person most skilled at convincing us that we are innocent...
is us.
Jesus refuses to let us hide behind the technicalities.

In Matthew 5:27–28, Christ takes His listeners beyond the outward act of adultery and confronts what can happen within the heart. The crucial Greek expression includes the words “πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν” — language describing looking with lustful desire or intent.
Jesus is not teaching that noticing someone is attractive automatically makes a married person an adulterer.
He is exposing something deeper.
Intentional, cultivated lust matters before God.
There is a difference between temptation arriving at your door and you inviting it inside, feeding it dinner, giving it a password, and wondering why it refuses to leave.
There is a difference between encountering an attractive woman and deliberately pursuing her attention.
There is a difference between an ordinary conversation and secretly building romantic intimacy.
There is a difference between temptation...
and courtship.

If you already have a wife and you are intentionally courting another woman—seeking her romantic affection, cultivating sexual desire, feeding emotional intimacy that belongs within your marriage, or positioning yourself as though you were available—then you cannot make the problem disappear simply by saying, “But we never had sex.”
Jesus goes after the heart because eventually the feet tend to follow where the heart has been permitted to wander.
And perhaps the most frightening part is that your wife may not know.
But God does.
Malachi 2:14 gives marriage language that should make every married man stop.
The Hebrew text describes the wife as the wife of your “בְּרִיתֶךָ” — beritekha — “your covenant.”
Not merely your girlfriend.
Not merely the woman sharing your surname.
Not merely the mother of your children.
Your covenant wife.
Malachi says that the LORD Himself was witness between a man and “the wife of your youth,” condemning treachery against that covenant relationship.
Think about that.
When nobody sees the messages...
God sees.
When your wife believes you are merely busy...
God knows where your attention is going.
When you carefully choose words that allow you to say, “Technically, I didn't lie”...
God knows the truth you were trying not to say.
When you erase the conversation...
you have erased nothing from His sight.
Marriage is not simply an arrangement between two people.
It is covenant.
And covenant changes the question.
The question is no longer merely, “How far can I go before it technically becomes adultery?”
The better question is:
“How faithfully can I love the woman I promised to love?”
That sounds completely different.
Hebrews 13:4 tells believers to hold marriage in honor and warns that God judges sexual immorality and adultery.
Honor.
That word leaves very little room for secret romantic auditions.
A faithful husband does not need to hate every other woman.
He does not need to avoid ordinary human interaction.
He does not become sinful merely because temptation occurs.
But he must learn where his heart belongs.
Because fidelity is bigger than avoiding somebody else's bed.
Faithfulness says:
My wife does not have to compete with women who were never supposed to have access to my romantic heart.
And Scripture does not merely tell husbands what to avoid.
It tells them whom to pursue.
“Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her.” — Ephesians 5:25.
Read that slowly.
Christ did not call you merely to remain technically married.
He called you to love.
Sacrificially.
Deliberately.
Faithfully.
Christlike love asks something radically different from the wandering heart.
While lust asks, “What can she give me?”
Christlike love asks, “What can I give for her good?”
While secret courtship searches for another woman's admiration, covenant love turns home and asks, “How can I cherish the woman God has entrusted to me?”
While lust wants novelty, Christlike love learns faithfulness.
While temptation whispers, “You deserve something new,” covenant says, “Remember what you promised.”
And Proverbs gives married desire somewhere beautiful to go.
“Rejoice in the wife of your youth.”
The passage continues by telling the husband to remain captivated by her love.
Notice what Scripture does.
It does not merely say, “Stop looking elsewhere.”
It says, in effect:
Come home.
Rejoice again.
Remember her.
Pursue her.
Cherish her.
Perhaps somewhere along the years, something changed.
Bills arrived.
Children cried.
Bodies aged.
Arguments accumulated.
Affection became routine.
You stopped dating each other.
You became excellent partners in surviving life but terrible students of one another's hearts.
Then another woman laughed at your jokes.
She noticed you.
She listened.
She complimented you.
And suddenly you felt twenty-five again.
Be careful.
Feeling alive is not always evidence that something is from God.
Sometimes temptation feels exhilarating precisely because sin is offering pleasure without showing you the invoice.
It shows you the secret messages.
It does not show you your wife crying in the bathroom.
It shows you the excitement.
It does not show you your children asking why Daddy doesn't live there anymore.
It shows you a woman at her most attractive.
It does not show you two damaged families sorting through consequences.
Sin is a terrible salesman.
It advertises the moment and hides the aftermath.
And maybe you are reading this thinking:
Too late.
Maybe it has already gone beyond messages.
Maybe there was a kiss.
Maybe there was a hotel.
Maybe there has been another relationship for months.
Maybe your wife already discovered it.
Maybe your marriage is hanging by a thread.
Maybe the man reading these words is not merely tempted.
Maybe you already fell.
Then hear this carefully.
The Gospel is not permission to continue sinning.
But neither is your sin greater than the blood of Jesus Christ.
This is where Christianity becomes breathtaking.
Jesus does not expose sin because He delights in destroying sinners.
He exposes darkness so sinners can come into the light.
Repentance is not saying, “I'm sorry I got caught.”
Repentance is not crying tonight and messaging her again next week.
Repentance is not asking God to remove consequences while protecting the secret relationship that created them.
Repentance turns.
It tells the truth.
It stops feeding the sin.
It stops romanticizing what God calls you to forsake.
It seeks forgiveness.
It accepts accountability.
It begins rebuilding what deception damaged.
And where necessary, it seeks wise pastoral and professional help to walk through the wreckage honestly.
Grace does not tell you that betrayal did not matter.
Grace tells you that betrayal does not have to write the final chapter.
Look at the cross.
There you see both the seriousness of sin and the magnitude of mercy.
Jesus did not die because sin was harmless.
He died because sin was deadly.
And He rose because death would not have the last word.
Maybe you became the scandal.
Maybe everybody thought you were the faithful husband.
Maybe you served at church.
Posted Bible verses.
Said grace before meals.
Called yourself a Christian.
And still entertained another woman's heart behind your wife's back.
There may be no comfortable way to hear this:
religious appearance cannot substitute for repentance.
But neither should shame convince you to run away from Christ.
Run toward Him.
Confess.
Repent.
Cut off what keeps pulling you back.
Stop protecting your reputation more fiercely than your marriage.
Stop asking whether you can keep the other woman “as a friend” when you know exactly what that relationship has become inside your heart.
Stop asking God to bless the very doorway through which temptation keeps entering.
And then...
go home.
Not merely to the house.
Go home with your heart.
Look at your wife again.
Not as the obstacle standing between you and excitement.
Not as the woman who became ordinary.
Not as the person whose weaknesses you have memorized while another woman's weaknesses remain conveniently hidden.
See her as a human being who trusted you with something precious.
Her heart.
Her years.
Her vulnerability.
Her covenant.
And if you have wounded her, understand this too:
you cannot demand that she heal according to your timetable.
Forgiveness and restored trust are related, but they are not identical.
You may confess in one evening.
Trust may take much longer to rebuild.
Real repentance is willing to walk that road without complaining that the consequences are inconvenient.
Because repentance does not ask only, “How can I feel forgiven?”
It also asks, “How can I begin becoming trustworthy?”
And husbands, Scripture gives us a terrifyingly beautiful standard:
Christ.
“Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her.”
Not Hollywood.
Not pornography.
Not your coworkers.
Not your divorced friends.
Not the algorithm feeding you endless images of women who never ask anything difficult from you.
Christ.
The One who gave Himself.
The One whose love was faithful.
The One whose love was sacrificial.
The One who did not abandon His bride when loving her became costly.
That is the direction.
And perhaps this article was not meant only for the man already cheating.
Perhaps it found the man standing three steps before the cliff.
You have her number.
The conversations are getting personal.
Your wife doesn't know.
Nothing physical has happened.
Yet.
Then brother...
this may be mercy arriving before catastrophe.
Delete what needs deleting.
End what needs ending.
Establish boundaries.
Tell the truth where truth must be told.
Seek mature Christian accountability.
Pray.
Open Scripture.
Court your wife again.
Take her somewhere.
Listen without holding your phone.
Learn what has been hurting her.
Ask what makes her feel loved.
Repent of the distance you helped create.
And remember why you chose her.
Do not wait until another man appreciates what you neglected before realizing what was sitting across the dinner table all along.
And wives reading this...
this is not permission to carry responsibility for your husband's choices.
You cannot manufacture another person's faithfulness by becoming prettier, quieter, thinner, more sexual, less emotional, or endlessly accommodating.
Each person answers before God for his or her own choices.
Marriage needs grace from both people.
But adultery is not cured by making the betrayed spouse responsible for preventing betrayal.
The unfaithful heart must repent.
And the wounded heart deserves truth, patience, and care.
Be honest before God first.
Or perhaps:
“No more hiding.”
Maybe you have not crossed the physical line, but you know your heart has been wandering.
Say it:
“Guard my marriage, Lord.”
Someone reading the same comment section may discover that they are not the only person fighting for repentance, restoration, and a marriage that nearly disappeared beneath secrecy.
Not because saving a post makes anyone holy.
Come back when the message arrives.
Come back when loneliness starts negotiating.
Come back when your mind whispers, “Nobody will ever know.”
And remember:
God already does.
Your share might reach him before the hotel room does.
Send it privately if that is wiser.

And if you know a couple struggling beneath betrayal, don't weaponize these words against them. Pray for them. Walk with them. Encourage wise pastoral care, accountability, and appropriate counseling.
Truth should perform surgery, not become another weapon.
Gospel Warrior exists to keep putting Christ-centered biblical truth where wounded, wandering, curious, and spiritually hungry people can encounter it.

Scripture teaches that Gospel ministry may receive material support; Paul writes that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive their living from Gospel ministry. But Scripture also protects giving from manipulation: believers are to give according to what they have decided in their hearts, “not reluctantly or under compulsion.”
It does not purchase salvation.
It does not replace repentance.
Jesus cannot be bought.
Grace cannot be purchased.
The Gospel is not for sale.

But if this ministry is feeding you spiritually and you genuinely want to glorify God by helping biblical truth reach farther, supporting Gospel Warrior is one practical way you can participate in that work.
Pray.
Follow.
Save.
Send it privately to someone who needs it.
Sometimes one share reaches a marriage you will never know you helped protect.
One comment tells a struggling believer, “You are not fighting alone.”
One saved article becomes tomorrow's reminder.
One invitation brings somebody closer to Scripture.
And one honest moment of repentance can change the direction of a family.
But after all of this, do not leave remembering Gospel Warrior more than you remember Jesus.
Because Gospel Warrior cannot save your marriage.
A comment cannot forgive adultery.
A shared post cannot regenerate your heart.
Only Christ saves.
Only His blood atones for sin.
Only His grace can take guilty people who genuinely repent and begin rewriting lives that seemed beyond repair.
So if you are married and courting another woman, stop asking how close you can stand to adultery without technically falling into it.
Turn around.
There is a covenant behind you.
There may still be a wife waiting for the man who once promised himself to her.
And above everything else, there is a Savior calling sinners out of darkness—not merely into better behavior, but into Himself.
The story does not have to end with deleted messages.
It does not have to end with another woman's perfume.
It does not have to end with children divided between homes.
It does not have to end with your wife wondering why she was not enough.
It does not have to end with you becoming permanently defined by the worst thing you ever did.
But something must die.
The secrecy.
The excuses.
The double life.
The fantasy.
The entitlement.
The version of you that keeps asking Jesus to forgive what you are still planning to continue.
Bring that man to the cross.
And let Christ begin making something new from what sin nearly destroyed.
Because sometimes the greatest love story is not finding another woman.
Sometimes it is becoming faithful again to the woman whose hand you already promised never to let go.
